clinicalPearls: Temporomandibular disorders are a group of musculoskeletal conditions affecting the jaw joints, the muscles of mastication, or both
Typical features are jaw pain, joint sounds such as clicking or crepitus, limited or deviated mouth opening, and pain on chewing
Pain is often localised to the preauricular region and may radiate to the temple, ear, or face, and can mimic ear or dental pathology
Most cases are muscular (myofascial) rather than intra-articular, and parafunctional habits like clenching and grinding are common contributors
Disc displacement with reduction typically produces reciprocal clicking, whereas displacement without reduction causes locking and restricted opening
It is largely a clinical diagnosis; imaging is reserved for atypical, persistent, or red-flag presentations
Initial management is conservative, including reassurance, jaw rest, soft diet, physiotherapy, occlusal splints, and stress and habit control
Psychological factors, stress, and chronic pain behaviours strongly influence symptoms and treatment response
reference.pathophysiology: Temporomandibular disorders arise from a multifactorial interplay of biomechanical overload, parafunctional habits, trauma, and psychosocial stress acting on the masticatory system. Sustained muscle hyperactivity from clenching or grinding produces myofascial pain and fatigue, while abnormal loading and internal derangement of the joint can disturb the normal disc-condyle relationship, causing clicking, locking, or degenerative change. Central sensitisation and psychological factors can amplify and perpetuate pain. The result is a spectrum ranging from purely muscular pain to intra-articular disc displacement and degenerative joint disease.
additionalDifferentials: Odontogenic pain from pulpal or periapical disease
Trigeminal neuralgia or other neuropathic facial pain
Giant cell (temporal) arteritis in older patients
Referred pain from cervical spine or headache disorders
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of jaw movement, joint sounds, and muscle tenderness
Evaluation of occlusion and parafunctional habits
MRI for suspected internal derangement when symptoms persist
CT or cone-beam imaging for bony or degenerative joint changes
Inflammatory markers if temporal arteritis is a concern in older patients
redFlags: New onset facial pain with headache, scalp tenderness, or visual symptoms in an older patient suggesting giant cell arteritis
Progressive limitation of opening, a hard end-feel, or a mass suggesting joint ankylosis or neoplasia
Unilateral worsening symptoms with cranial nerve signs pointing to a sinister cause
Recent significant trauma raising the possibility of condylar fracture
reference.prognosis: Most patients improve with conservative, reversible measures and the condition often follows a self-limiting or fluctuating course, though a minority develop chronic pain or progressive degenerative joint change.
pitfalls: Proceeding to irreversible occlusal or surgical treatment before trying conservative care
Missing giant cell arteritis in an older patient with jaw and temporal symptoms
Attributing all facial pain to the joint and overlooking dental or neuropathic causes
Neglecting parafunctional habits and psychosocial factors that drive symptoms
